label: Title
notes: Open Chapter 10 as the lower-curvature companion to the preceding upper-bound chapter. The first promise is local: a small fan of angles around one point can certify a curvature lower bound. The second promise is global: once Toponogov is available, comparison geometry produces rigidity, diameter control, splitting, dimension information, volume comparison, and compactness behavior. Point students to the notebook and to printed pages 351-404 so the lecture feels anchored in the assigned source span.

label: Local Quadruple Fan
notes: The local quadruple condition is the first working test. Given four nearby points, compare the model angles that would be seen from one vertex and ask whether the angle fan is too large. For lower curvature bounds, the geometry refuses to fold inward beyond the model allowance. Emphasize that this is a local diagnostic, not yet the full Toponogov theorem.

label: Hinge Comparison
notes: A hinge is the simplest global comparison unit: two geodesic sides with an included angle. In a curvature-bounded-below space, the side opposite the hinge is controlled by the corresponding model triangle. The point of the slide is to turn the abstract curvature hypothesis into a concrete measurement game: fix two sides and an angle, then compare the third side.

label: Examples
notes: Use examples to keep the definition from becoming too ethereal. Smooth Riemannian manifolds with sectional curvature bounded below fit the theory, but so do many singular length spaces such as suitable polyhedra, convex surfaces, cones with valid links, and quotients by isometric group actions. The examples are not decoration; they tell students where singular tangent cones will come from later.

label: Cone Links
notes: Cone links are the chapter's local microscope. A cone is lower-curvature controlled when its angular link has the right diameter and comparison behavior. This is why spaces of directions matter: they are not an extra object added after the fact, but the data that controls the first-order cone model around a point.

label: Quotients And Convex Surfaces
notes: Quotients and convex surfaces are natural factories for examples. Convex surfaces inherit lower curvature behavior from the ambient Euclidean comparison picture, while quotients preserve comparison only when the action behaves metrically well. Stress the stabilizer issue: a quotient may be perfectly legitimate but still acquire singular directions at fixed points.

label: Toponogov Engine
notes: Toponogov is the global engine of the chapter. Local comparison information is upgraded to a statement about geodesic triangles and hinges across the space. The theorem is the reason lower curvature becomes a machine rather than a definition: once triangle sides and angles are comparable to the model space, many global consequences can be pushed through.

label: Downstream Theorems
notes: This slide is a dependency map. Rather than presenting diameter, splitting, dimension, volume, limits, and tangent cones as a bag of theorems, read them as outputs of comparison plus compactness and local structure. The proof-dependency artifact should help students see which later results are powered directly by Toponogov and which require additional regularity tools.

label: Diameter Control
notes: Diameter control is the first rigidity consequence to emphasize. A positive lower curvature bound makes very large spaces impossible under the right hypotheses, and equality cases force model-like behavior. The important teaching move is to separate the inequality from the rigidity statement: the number bounds size, while equality describes geometry.

label: Splitting
notes: Splitting is the opposite kind of rigidity: a line in a nonnegatively curved lower-bound setting forces a product decomposition. Present the line as a global geodesic witness that forbids hidden bending. Once the line exists, Busemann-type functions and comparison inequalities organize the space into a factor along the line and a transverse factor.

label: Dimension
notes: Dimension in Alexandrov spaces is subtle because points can be singular, but it is still robust. Strainers provide coordinate-like data, and spaces of directions keep local dimension under control. Tell students that dimension here is not merely topological bookkeeping; it is detected by comparison configurations that behave like almost orthogonal directions.

label: Bishop Volume Comparison
notes: Bishop-type volume comparison translates curvature lower bounds into monotonicity of volume ratios. The slide should be taught as a quantitative companion to the qualitative rigidity theorems. Curvature prevents too much spreading, and equality or near equality signals that the metric balls are behaving like their model counterparts.

label: GH Limit Collapse
notes: Gromov-Hausdorff limits show why the category matters. Lower curvature bounds are stable under appropriate limits, but dimension may collapse and singular sets may appear. The figure lets students see the main tension: comparison survives, while ordinary smooth intuition can fail dramatically under limiting processes.

label: Strainers
notes: Strainers are the local coordinate technology of the chapter. A collection of pairs acts like approximate coordinate axes when comparison angles are close to the Euclidean pattern. Students should understand them as a measurable way to say that a point has enough independent directions to look regular at a chosen scale.

label: Spaces Of Directions
notes: Spaces of directions collect germs of geodesics issuing from a point, with angular distance between them. They are themselves metric spaces with curvature behavior inherited from the original space. The pedagogical point is that singularity is visible in the direction space before it is visible in the whole neighborhood.

label: Tangent Cones
notes: The tangent cone is the blow-up limit: rescale distances near a point and watch the local geometry become conical. At a smooth point the cone is Euclidean, while at a singular point the cone records the link and any missing directions. Connect this slide back to cones, strainers, and spaces of directions so the last definitions feel inevitable.

label: Recap And Opening Topics
notes: Close by naming the arc of the lecture. Lower curvature begins as an angle-fan test, becomes a hinge and triangle comparison theorem, and then drives rigidity, volume, compactness, and singular local models. The opening topics for discussion are where the smooth theorems still survive, where singularities force new language, and why tangent cones are the right next microscope.
